title: Teachers of the World, Unite to Get Reading Right
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Harriett Janetos uses a public disagreement over Daniel Kliger's modifications to the Core Knowledge Language Arts curriculum to argue for a professional norm: teachers must have right reasons they can explain to other professionals, and know where the science ends and their judgment begins. She summarises Kliger's critique that CKLA gives second graders too little connected reading and too little meaning-building, with her own comments on each point. She notes Natalie Wexler's concerns about weakening a strong curriculum but argues that Wexler's concessions deserved more prominence. Janetos holds that validating a process is not validating a conclusion, and asks educators to unite behind explained decisions, not uniformity. She adds that being wrong should fuel progress and not humiliation.
points: The central standard is that teachers need explainable 'right' reasons and an honest sense of where research ends and judgment begins.
Kliger argues CKLA offers too little actual reading in K-2, relies on decodables, and does not build conceptual connections; Janetos annotates each point with supporting research.
Janetos argues Wexler's critique left out concessions she made in the comments, and that respect for Kliger's analysis was missing.
Validating a teacher's reasoning process is not the same as agreeing with the conclusion; each proposal can be taken, tweaked or tossed.
She argues unity does not require uniformity, and that being wrong is how a profession learns.
quotes: My obligation in this discussion was to express in return the reasons supporting my position that explain why I drew those conclusions because I really do believe that each of us is required to have ‘right’ reasons that we can explain to other professionals.
Good teachers use both individual teaching expertise and the best available external evidence, and neither alone is enough.
Knowledge-rich is a starting place. It’s necessary but not sufficient. It’s not good enough.
Unity does not mean uniformity; nor does it mean unanimous agreement. It simply means uniting under the obligation to have the right reasons for what we do that we can explain to other professionals.
The Knowledge Matters Campaign is to be commended for making a convincing case for the crucial role knowledge plays in comprehension. It is no longer a whether but a how.
But—validation of a process is not validation of a person’s point of view; it doesn’t mean Daniel Kliger is right.
But being wrong should not be a source of humiliation. Wrongness fuels the engine of progress.
